## Why the papers' greedy is not exact {#sec-greedy}

Both papers schedule each fixed multiset of landings (a PPP) greedily and claim the result is the
optimal makespan of that PPP. Their own words are in the grey boxes; §5 of the note gives the
counterexamples, and the smallest one is checked by the Lean kernel.

### The greedy counterexample {#node-s5}

**Lean** [informal]{.badge .informal} (parts in Lean) · **Note** [proof in the note]{.badge .informal} · **Hypotheses** (S), (A1) · **Uses** [4.8](#node-corollary-4-8)

::: {.from-paper}
**From the original paper** (Quemy & Schoenauer, EvoCOP 2015, §2.3 *Computing the Shortest Makespan*, HAL preprint hal-01109777v1, pp. 5–6).

> **Step 1: Handling P3-free PPPs** […] For a PPP with $\beta = 0$, greedy Algorithm 1 dispatches the
> longest flight durations first, assigning them to the available planes with shortest 'private'
> makespan (who have yet flown the less), ending with the one-way last flights from $C_I$ to $C_G$
> (planes end in $C_G$). The algorithm returns the flight durations $(D^1_k)$ for all planes $k$ (to be
> used in the second step), and the optimal makespan for the subproblem is obviously
> $\max_k(D^1_k)$.
>
> **Step 2: Tackling Patterns P3** The second step consists in dispatching the durations of P3
> patterns among the planes according to their previous flight durations $(D^1_k)_{k=1,\dots,p}$, by
> sequentially assigning the longest P3 flight to the two planes with the smallest current flight
> durations. This can be performed greedily again, with a slightly modified version of the
> Algorithm 1, if we only consider the flight durations.

```
Algorithm 1  Computing the optimal makespan of PPP (e, w) when β = 0
i ← 1 ; j ← 1               {Indices of cities in e and w resp., longest durations first}
D_k ← 0, k = 1, ..., p                             {'Private' makespan for plane k}
S_k ← EAST, k = 1, ..., p                     {All planes are in C_I, going eastward}
while j ≤ t − p do
  k ← ArgMin_i(D_i)                 {Plane with shortest private makespan, in C_I or C_G}
  if S_k = EAST then
    D_k ← D_k + 2d_{e_i}                          {From C_I to C_G through city C_{e_i}}
    S_k ← WEST ; i ← i + 1
  else
    D_k ← D_k + 2d_{w_j}                          {From C_G to C_I through city C_{w_j}}
    S_k ← EAST ; j ← j + 1
  end if
end while                                     {Are there persons and planes left in C_I?}
while i ≤ t do
  k ← ArgMin_{i; S_i=EAST} (D_i)              {Plane in C_I with shortest private makespan}
  D_k ← D_k + 2d_{e_i}                            {From C_I to C_G through city C_{e_i}}
  S_k ← WEST ; i ← i + 1
end while
return (D_k)_{k=1,...,p}          {All private makespans are needed for the second step}
Makespan (e, w) = max_{k=1,...,p} {D_k}
```
:::

::: {.from-paper}
**From the original paper** (Quemy & Schoenauer, EvoCOP 2015, §2.3, HAL preprint hal-01109777v1, p. 7).

> **Proposition**: For a given PPP $C$ and $\beta_{\rm set}$, the algorithm returns the optimal
> makespan.
>
> **Proof**: The incompressible time to transport all passengers, according to a given
> $\beta_{\rm set}$ is $T = 4\sum_{i\in\beta_{\rm set}} d_i + 2\sum_{i\in\{e',w'\}} d_i$. A theoretical
> optimal plan with this pattern repartition is a plan without any waiting point for any plane. The
> above algorithm gives the optimal distribution of the set of times into $p$. Then, if a plan can be
> constructed with such a makespan, it is optimal for the PPP and the repartition of patterns. As it
> exists a method to construct such a plan, we can conclude that the algorithm is optimal for the PPP
> $C$ and $\beta_{\rm set}$. $\square$
:::

::: {.our-work}
**Statement** (theory note, §5).

Both papers prove optimality of a greedy that assigns the longest durations first to the least-loaded plane.
The proof (arXiv §3.2) rests on the sentence "the above algorithm gives the optimal distribution of the set
of times into $p$". The no-waiting construction is correct (Theorem 4.1); the optimal distribution is not.

* $d = (6, 10)$, $p = 2$, $t = 5$, PPP $a = (10,10,6,6,6)$, $\bar a = (10,6,6)$: the greedy gives every
  plane a 20-crossing first and ends at 52/68. The partition $\{10,10,10\} \mid \{6,6,6,6,6\}$ gives 60/60.
  The front point (260, 60) is missed.
* $d = (1,3)$, $c = (9,5)$, $t = 4$, $p = 2$: the point (42, 12) needs the plane making the drop-off to also
  take the long crossing; the no-duplicate greedy ends at 14.

Deciding $M(X) \le 2T$ is strongly NP-complete (Theorem 8.1), so no polynomial greedy can be exact unless
P = NP.

**In Lean.** `lptCounterexample_front` is the exact front of `d = (6, 10)`, `c = (40, 20)`, `t = 5`, `p = 2`, for every table of central flights, checked by `decide +kernel` (no compiled code is trusted). It contains `(260, 60)`. That the 2016 greedy misses this point is the hand computation of the note (52/68 instead of 60/60) and the recorded output of the 2016 solver; it is not a Lean statement.

**Formalised parts.** These declarations cover part of the statement; the node keeps the status of the note.

*Part* `ZenoFront.Examples.lptCounterexample_front` [machine-checked]{.badge .ok}

```lean
/-- **The exact front of the LPT counterexample**, checked by the kernel: for every table of
central flight durations, the Pareto front of `d = (6, 10)`, `c = (40, 20)`, `t = 5`, `p = 2`
is `(320, 48), (280, 56), (260, 60), (240, 64), (200, 72), (160, 80)`. In particular the point
`(260, 60)`, which the papers' greedy misses, is on the front. -/
theorem lptCounterexample_front (dc : Fin 2 → Fin 2 → ℕ) :
    IsParetoFront (achievable ⟨![6, 10], ![6, 10], dc⟩ ![40, 20] 5 2)
      [(320, 48), (280, 56), (260, 60), (240, 64), (200, 72), (160, 80)] := …
```

[`lean/ZenoFront/Examples.lean`, lines 96–103](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/f8186577c0d0639e0659f4fb9debc62b9a5d35e1/lean/ZenoFront/Examples.lean#L96-L103){.lean-src} (statement only; the proof is elided)

:::

::: {.strengthen}
**What fails.** "The above algorithm gives the optimal distribution of the set of times into $p$" is
false: longest-first onto the least-loaded plane is a heuristic (LPT), not an exact partition, and the
landings of a PPP must in addition be split so that the partition is *admissible*. Deciding whether a
multiset of landings can be flown within a makespan is strongly NP-complete (Theorem 8.1), so no
polynomial per-PPP rule can be exact unless P = NP. The no-waiting construction itself is correct
(Theorem 4.1).
:::
